prime.problem: Traffic rises and falls, but a rented GPU bills the same busy or idle. Provision for the peak and most paid hours serve nothing; scale down aggressively and the next spike waits for a replica that takes seconds or ten minutes to start.
prime.fits: Builds on cost-per-token's busy share u: every price there assumed a GPU that is always busy. This card is about raising u without breaking latency, and the cold start is what limits how far you can push it.
expect: Kiely's five autoscaler knobs and two signals
the four parts of a cold start
weight loading = bytes ÷ bandwidth, tier by tier
prime.goal: Price a traffic day under different autoscaling policies, break a cold start into its parts and compute the one you can compute exactly, and decide how many warm replicas to keep.

attend: Why is utilization a lagging signal and traffic a leading one?
Which of the four cold-start parts can you compute exactly, and which dominates once the weights are close by?
Autoscaling at all saves 48% on the example day; scale to zero saves only another $23.94. Why so little?
Why does ServerlessLLM migrate a running request's tokens rather than its KV cache?
When is a pay-per-token API cheaper than any autoscaling policy?

must: A GPU-hour bills whether or not it serves → $/M = p × 10⁶ ÷ (3600 × capacity × u) → provisioning for the peak on a bursty day runs at u = 36% ($0.48/M vs $0.17 when busy) → autoscaling exists to raise u

You can only remove replicas you can quickly bring back → a cold start = GPU procurement + image + weights + engine warm-up, in series → from 616 s (fresh node, 1 Gbps, uncached compile) to 10 s (weights in host DRAM) → the cold start sets how thin the warm floor can be

During a cold start, traffic above capacity queues → backlog = excess tok/s × cold-start time, drained only by the spare capacity after the new replica is up → a 10-minute start leaves users queued ~49 minutes; a warm spare costs $95.76/day and removes it

Weight loading is bytes ÷ bandwidth → the storage tier moves it 500× (16 GB: 128 s at 1 Gbps, 0.25 s over PCIe 5) and FP8 halves every row → once weights are close, the engine's compile and CUDA-graph capture is most of what's left, so cache those too
elevated: ServerlessLLM moves a request's token ids (KB) instead of its KV cache (GB) and recomputes the KV at the destination → recomputing 1,000 tokens costs about as much as generating 100 → migration is cheap enough to load a model on the busy server that already has its checkpoint
reference: Kiely's knob names (min/max replicas, window, scale-down delay, concurrency target)
ServerlessLLM's 3.6–8.2× loader and 10–200× headline with its testbed caveat
the bursty day's hourly replica counts

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the cold-start timeline as four stacked blocks with a fast and a slow example for each, then write the one formula that ties utilization to $/M and one sentence on why the warm floor exists.
checklist: GPU procurement (warm pool ≈ 0 vs a fresh node, minutes)
weights = bytes ÷ bandwidth (PCIe 5 0.25 s vs 1 Gbps 128 s for 16 GB)
engine startup (cached compile seconds vs uncached minutes)
$/M = p·10⁶ ÷ (3600·c·u); a floor of warm replicas trades idle $ for no cold start on the first user

retrieve.q: Explain why fast cold starts are what make aggressive scale-down safe.
answer: scale-down leaves less headroom for the next spike
during a cold start, excess traffic queues and must be drained afterwards
short cold starts shrink that backlog, so you can keep fewer idle replicas (Kiely: slow starts lead to over-provisioning)

retrieve.q: Walk through the tuned cold start for the 8B: which parts are near zero, why, and where the 33.2 s goes.
answer: engine: cached compile, 30 s (illustrative): most of the total

retrieve.q: Compare provision-for-peak, min 1 replica, and scale to zero on the example day. Which would you pick for a customer-facing chat app, and why?
answer: peak: $383/day, 35.6% utilization, never a cold start
min 1: $199.50/day, 68.4%, no user ever waits a cold start
zero: $175.56/day, 77.7%, but the first morning user waits a whole cold start
min 1: $23.94/day is cheap insurance for a latency-sensitive app

compare.q: A cold start after a scale-up and a failover after a GPU dies both need a replica that isn't serving yet. What is the same mechanism, and how does a warm spare change each?
answer: both wait for GPU + image + weights + engine before a replica serves
scale-up: the cost is queueing during the start; failure: the cost is users dropped until a replacement is up
a warm spare with weights loaded turns both into seconds or minutes, at the price of idle GPU-hours

compare.q: CUDA graphs made each decode step faster in course 3; here they make the cold start slower. What is being traded, and how do engines get both?
answer: capturing one graph per batch size costs time at startup
in exchange, each step avoids per-kernel launch overhead for the life of the replica
engines cache the captured/compiled artifacts so a new replica reuses them (same GPU type, CUDA and dependencies only)

predict.q: Replace the bursty day with a flat one: exactly 12,900 tok/s all 24 hours, which two replicas can serve. Commit: how much cheaper is autoscaling (min 1) than provisioning for the peak now?
predict.answer: Not cheaper at all. Both keep exactly 2 replicas all day: 48 GPU-hours, $191.52, and u = 100%, so $0.172/M. Autoscaling only saves the hours between the peak and the valleys; with no valleys, every policy converges on the same count (the card's flat-day try-this).

apply.task: Serve the 8B in FP8 instead (8.03 GB of weights) and keep the card's illustrative non-weight times (naive: 300 s GPU + 8 s image + 180 s engine; tuned: 30 s engine; best: 10 s engine). (1) Compute the three cold starts, loading weights at 1 Gbps, 5 GB/s and 64 GB/s. (2) For the card's burst (18,000 tok/s arriving with 12,900 tok/s of capacity, and 1,350 tok/s spare once the third replica is up), compute the backlog and drain time for each. (3) Did FP8 matter more for the naive or the tuned setup?
apply.done: (1) 552.2 s, 31.6 s, 10.1 s. (2) Backlog 2.82M / 0.16M / 0.05M tokens; drain 2,086 s / 119 s / 38 s. (3) In seconds, naive (−64 s of 616); in share, tuned (−1.6 s of 33.2, but the engine's 30 s now dominates even more): the next win is caching the engine, not smaller weights.
apply.hint: 1 Gbps = 0.125 GB/s. Backlog = (18,000 − 12,900) × cold start; drain = backlog ÷ 1,350.
